note: COMPUTED FROM HUMAN TRIAL-LEVEL DATA, superseding the author estimates. Source: the Confidence Database (Rahnev et al., osf.io/s46pr), dataset data_Desender_2021_Cognit.csv, from Desender, K., Donner, T. H. & Verguts, T. (2021), 'Dynamic expressions of confidence within an evidence accumulation framework', Cognition 207:104522, doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2020.104522 (22,080 trials, n=30). THIS DATASET WAS CHOSEN BECAUSE ITS COHERENCE LEVELS MATCH THIS PORT'S. It tests motion coherence at .05, .1, .2 and .4, which are four of this port's five levels (.05, .10, .20, .40, .80). Of the 43 dot-motion datasets in the Confidence Database it is the only one whose coherence set aligns this closely. Trials are restricted to non-training, non-volatile (Volatility = 0) trials with a valid response, and the 0% coherence trials are dropped since this port has none: 6,343 trials from 30 participants. Per-coherence accuracy, mean across participants: .05 -> 0.637 (sd 0.103), .10 -> 0.770 (sd 0.113), .20 -> 0.897 (sd 0.082), .40 -> 0.946 (sd 0.069). THE .80 LEVEL IS EXTRAPOLATED, NOT OBSERVED. A two-parameter Weibull with the 2AFC floor fixed at 0.5, p = 0.5 + 0.5*(1 - exp(-(c/alpha)^beta)), fits the four observed points at alpha = 0.137, beta = 0.997 and predicts 0.9985 at .80 - effectively ceiling, which is what 80% coherence should produce. Each participant's .80 value is their own .40 accuracy shifted by the group-level fitted difference, capped at 0.999. Values are then binned by this port's own rule (low = coherence <= 0.10, medium <= 0.20, high otherwise), giving low 0.704, medium 0.897, high 0.953, and an overall of 0.842 with the five levels weighted equally as this port presents them. SUPERSEDES 0.79 / 0.60 / 0.85 / 0.97, which were author estimates anchored to the Roitman & Shadlen shape after the earlier 'Pinet et al. (2024)' attribution was withdrawn as non-existent. The low-coherence bin was the furthest off (0.60 against 0.704). THE ALGORITHM-DEPENDENCE CAVEAT STILL APPLIES AND SHOULD BE STATED. Pilly & Seitz (2009), Vision Research 49(13):1599-1612, show that direction-discrimination accuracy depends on the noise algorithm, dot density, speed, aperture and duration, so any cross-implementation import carries error. Matching coherence levels removes the largest source of that error but not all of it; Desender's display parameters are not identical to this port's 200-dot, 2,000 ms canvas. This is now a matched-coherence empirical baseline rather than an estimate, and remains a candidate for replacement by on-platform human data. Roitman & Shadlen (2002), J. Neurosci. 22(21):9475-9490 remains the citation for the SHAPE across coherence, which is what the L3 signatures test; it is a two-macaque study and never constrained the human absolute level.
